File photo: Reuters/Nathan Howard In his recent speech to the Federalist Society, US secretary of state Marco Rubio defended President Donald Trump’s sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC). Rubio condemned the court as an illegitimate, unelected tribunal that claims authority over sovereign nations, including those that never accepted its jurisdiction.
 Yet in March 2022, then senator Rubio co-sponsored a Senate resolution that described the ICC as a tribunal that “seeks to uphold the rule of law” by investigating and trying individuals accused of the gravest international crimes. The resolution encouraged member states to petition the court to investigate Russian war crimes and crimes against humanity in Ukraine.
 Both Ukraine and the State of Palestine accepted ICC jurisdiction over crimes committed on their territories. But when the ICC sought to hold Israeli leaders accountable over Gaza, the administration responded with sanctions. Trump’s February 2025 executive order cited the court’s arrest warrants issued against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
 For the US, is international justice a principle to uphold, or merely a tool to use against its adversaries? - Terry Hansen, Wisconsin
